Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Djibouti's rural primary health centres (38 facilities) operate in a pyramidal system. No evidence found of EMR or digital patient records/registers/prescriptions at clinic level. Djibouti uses DHIS2 for HMIS, with recent IGAD digital equipment donations to districts/HIS. World Bank Health Strengthening Project reports 84% facilities with DHIS2 data entry; some enter directly, others use paper and submit immediately; manual disaggregated data collection noted. Indicates predominant paper-based recording at rural clinics with aggregate digital entry (some direct), fitting score 2. Lacks rural-specific data but general facility mix and absence of EMR evidence supports this over 1 or 3. World Bank ISR, IGAD, WHO EMRO private health

revision_notes: Original Value Code (1, Entirely paper) is confirmed. The Comments field itself argued for a score of 2 based on a World Bank ISR reference to '84% facilities with DHIS2 data entry', but this appears to describe data availability at district/regional HIS level rather than capture at the point of care. A more specific and recent source, UNICEF's MENARO Djibouti country brief (December 2024), states explicitly that although DHIS2 has the technical capacity to include community-level data, this integration 'has not yet' occurred, that there are 'no community indicators and tools for collecting community data', and that plans to deploy medical secretaries for electronic data entry are a future step, not current practice. IGAD's December 2024 digital equipment handover targeted district health offices and HMIS/HIS units, not primary clinics themselves. On the balance of evidence, facility-level data capture in rural clinics remains paper-based, with digitisation occurring only once data is aggregated above facility level. Score of 1 confirmed.
revised_comments: Djibouti operates a pyramidal health system in which the Ministry of Health's DHIS2 platform serves as the national health management information system, aggregating routine data reported from health facilities. As of late 2024, DHIS2 does not yet incorporate data collection at community or primary-clinic level: a UNICEF regional country brief records that despite DHIS2's technical capacity for community-level data, this integration has not been implemented, and no community-level indicators or digital collection tools are currently in use at the point of care. Plans to introduce medical secretaries for electronic data entry, and a December 2024 donation of digital equipment from IGAD to district health offices and health information system units, point to future strengthening of the system at district and regional level rather than at the primary clinic itself. Data capture in Djibouti's rural primary healthcare clinics therefore continues to rely on paper registers and records, which are subsequently compiled and entered into DHIS2 at a higher administrative level.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Djibouti are managed by the National Gendarmerie, responsible for security outside Djibouti City. No evidence found of digital case management, incident reports, or complaints recording at rural facilities. Djiboutian law mandates handwritten procès-verbaux (police reports) and registers for garde à vue in police and gendarmerie stations, indicating paper-based initial recording. US State Dept 2020 HR report notes records digitalization only in certain urban National Police precincts (phased implementation), aimed at tracking arrestees; no mention for gendarmerie or rural areas. Police response slow, resources limited per OSAC reports. Casier judiciaire (criminal records) issued manually by Ministry of Justice. Recent digital initiatives (e.g., 2025 Digital Code, mobile ID) focus on public services/ID, not police case files. In francophone Africa, rural stations typically use paper procès-verbaux. Thus, predominantly paper at rural level, with possible urban digitization pilots.

revision_notes: Original Value Code (1, Entirely paper) confirmed. The original State Department PDF citation was inaccessible (site error) but its finding is consistent with newer sources: a 2025 market analysis of Djibouti's law enforcement software sector describes limited government investment and adoption of digital case-management, records-management or dispatch systems nationally, constrained by cost and local technical capacity. A September 2024 EU/Civipol procurement to supply laptops, tablets and servers to Djiboutian police and judicial authorities is targeted at specialised anti-trafficking/migration investigation units, not routine rural gendarmerie station operations, and in any case represents equipment procurement rather than deployed, in-use systems. No evidence found of digital case files, incident registers or complaints systems in use at rural stations. Score of 1 confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural policing in Djibouti falls under the National Gendarmerie, which is legally required to record procès-verbaux and garde-à-vue registers by hand. A 2025 industry assessment of Djibouti's law enforcement software market finds adoption of case-management, records-management and dispatch software still limited nationally, constrained by cost, infrastructure and local technical capacity, with most available solutions imported rather than deployed at scale. A 2024 donor-funded procurement of laptops, tablets and servers for police and judicial authorities is directed at specialised anti-trafficking investigation units rather than general rural station operations. Data capture in rural police and gendarmerie stations accordingly remains paper-based, with any digitisation confined to specific specialised or urban units.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Djibouti rural registry offices (interior regions: Tadjourah, Obock, Dikhil, Ali-Sabieh, Arta) record vital events in paper registers with no computers or internet (~2013 WHO assessment). Monthly stats sent physically to central. Low rural coverage (20%), poor access. Urban areas have databases for hospital births. 2019 RNPP biometric ID system assigns NNI to those in civil registries, implying paper data entry at higher levels later. No evidence of rural digital recording or pilots; plans for computers (2013) unconfirmed in recent sources. Thus, rural facilities entirely paper-based.

revision_notes: Original Value Code (1, Entirely paper) confirmed. The WHO EMRO CRVS document cited originally could not be retrieved (repeated timeout) so was not re-verified; UNICEF's CRVS country profile for Djibouti (fieldwork 2016-17, still the most detailed public account) records registration processing as 'manually (on paper)'. A 2024 article from the Ville de Djibouti confirms the capital operates a computerised civil status management system (SIGEC) since 2011 and commissioned an international diagnostic of it in April 2024, but this system is explicitly municipal/urban in scope. No evidence was found of an equivalent computerised system in the five interior regional prefectures (Tadjourah, Obock, Dikhil, Ali-Sabieh, Arta). The 2019 RNPP law centralises identity data nationally but operates above the level of the local registrar's office and does not itself digitise data capture at the counter. Score of 1 confirmed for rural registry offices specifically.
revised_comments: Civil registration in Djibouti's interior regions is carried out at prefecture-level registrar's offices using handwritten paper registers, with statistics forwarded physically to the central civil status administration. By contrast, the capital, Djibouti-Ville, has operated a computerised civil status management system (SIGEC) since 2011 and in 2024 commissioned an international expert diagnostic of this system with a view to modernisation and improved data security, an initiative confined to the municipality rather than the interior regions. No comparable computerised registration system has been documented for the rural prefectures, and national civil registration processing outside the capital is recorded as manual. The 2019 law establishing the biometric National Population Register (RNPP) centralises identity data at national level but does not digitise data capture at rural civil registry counters.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Djibouti use the OPAD digital application for data collection on administrative metrics like enrollment and outcomes, as per World Bank analysis. However, data is manually re-entered centrally due to system incompatibilities, causing 7-month delays in reporting. This suggests digital tools exist at point-of-service but are not fully integrated or reliable for routine use. No specific evidence confirms daily attendance or learning outcomes are recorded digitally at rural facilities; traditional paper registers likely persist alongside apps for aggregate reporting. EMIS supports national statistical yearbooks via the Ministry's Planning Department, but rural schools (avg. 120 students, smaller than urban 527) face infrastructure barriers like poor connectivity, electricity, and ICT skills, as inferred from general reports. World Bank project (2019) aims to modernize EMIS with real-time portals and student tracking, prioritizing urban rollout before 60-70% rural coverage, indicating current predominant paper with emerging digital pilots. Key barriers: technical incompatibilities, limited training, rural access issues. National EMIS ambition contrasts with rural reality of partial digitization focused on aggregation, not point-of-care recording. Score 2 reflects isolated digital use for reporting, not standard at most rural sites.

revision_notes: Original Value Code (1, Entirely paper) is revised to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) to align with the evidence, which the Comments field itself had already concluded pointed to a score of 2. The World Bank's 2019 Project Appraisal Document confirms school directors enter administrative data directly through the OPAD digital application at facility level, even though MENFOP subsequently re-keys this data centrally due to system incompatibility. A July 2024 USAID article confirms a tablet-based classroom observation tool, developed with FHI360, has been made mandatory nationwide for primary school inspections, with data transmitted directly to a central dashboard from the classroom. Both represent genuine digital data capture occurring at the facility, alongside continued paper-based record keeping for most routine functions (attendance, grades). A January 2024 Global Partnership for Education blog confirms a broader digital EMIS with unique student identifiers is still 'gradually being developed', i.e. not yet in general use. No rural-specific figures were found, so the assessment relies on general national practice; rural connectivity, electricity and ICT skills constraints (noted in the Oxford Business Group 2023 report) likely slow adoption relative to urban schools, supporting 'mostly paper' rather than 'mostly digital'.
revised_comments: Djibouti's primary schools use the OPAD (outil de pilotage d'aide à la décision) application, through which school directors enter enrolment and administrative data directly at facility level, and since 2024 a USAID-supported, tablet-based classroom observation tool has been made mandatory nationwide, with pedagogical advisors recording observations directly into a central dashboard during school visits. These represent genuine point-of-service digital data capture, but routine pupil records such as attendance and grades continue to be kept mainly on paper, and the Ministry of National Education and Vocational Training's broader digital education management platform, which will introduce unique student identifiers, remains at an early stage of development. Rural schools face additional constraints from limited connectivity, electricity supply and ICT skills relative to urban schools, which is likely to slow the pace of adoption. Overall, digital tools are used for specific functions at rural school facilities, while paper remains the predominant medium for day-to-day record keeping.
